Artificial turf on Dundee's ridge, from the depot to the new subdivisions

Kissimmee Artificial Turf installs synthetic lawns, pet turf and putting greens in Dundee, the citrus-and-rail town on US-27 about 23 miles from our Kissimmee base, at the same $8–$18 range as the rest of Central Florida. Dundee runs its own Development Services Department for building permits, separate from Polk County's office. As of September 2026, the town's own water utility answers to the district's Modified Phase III shortage order.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

A depot town on the ridge, not a subdivision suburb

Dundee was named in 1910 after a settler's hometown in Scotland, and the Atlantic Coast Line Railroad's arrival the following year, on its new Haines City-to-Sebring branch, turned a citrus crossroads into a town almost overnight (a historical marker on the depot grounds covers the full account). The 1912 depot on Main Street, the first stop built on that branch line, still stands today as the Margaret Kampsen Historic Depot Museum, and the packing house the Dundee Citrus Growers Association built beside the tracks in 1929 is a reminder that fruit, not rooftops, built this town first. The 2020 Census counted 5,235 residents (Census Bureau figures), a scale small enough that a single town office, not a county building complex, still handles the paperwork.

The lakes that set Dundee's turf setback

Dundee counts eight lakes within town limits, four of them open to the public, and three come up often on a turf job: 32-acre Lake Marie, next to the community center's own park and playground on Main Street; 21-acre Lake Menzie; and 407-acre Lake Annie, bordered on its east side by the Barbara B. Pedersen Wildlife Preserve (Polk County Water Atlas records). Florida's May 19, 2026 turf standard draws a 10-foot line around all three: no synthetic grass closer to the water than that, except behind an existing seawall or bulkhead, and none at all inside a drainage swale or a pond's own littoral zone (Rule 62-308.100). A lakefront lot on any of Dundee's public lakes usually has more usable yard than that line first suggests; it just isn't the strip closest to the shoreline.

New subdivisions on graded ridge lots

South of Haines City, Holiday Builders and DRB Homes are building Woodland Ranch Estates, a 116-acre subdivision on old grove land with homes priced from the high $200s (GrowthSpotter's coverage of the project). The native ground under that grading is Candler sand, excessively drained and rated very rapid to rapid in permeability, built from thick wind-blown and marine deposits with slopes that can run up to 12 percent on the ridge (the USDA's official series description). Fast-draining sand keeps a yard from pooling, but it also shifts more than the heavier soils to the south, which is why a base on a sloped Dundee lot gets compacted in careful lifts and every edge gets anchored against sliding, since the state rule's ban on infill washing off the property is a practical concern here, not just a paperwork line.

Who reviews a turf permit in Dundee

The Town of Dundee runs its own Development Services Department rather than routing permits through Polk County or a contracted plan-review firm, which puts it in different territory from several of the small towns around it. The office, at 124 Dundee Road, takes applications by downloaded form emailed to permits@townofdundee.com or a call to (863) 438-8330 (Development Services). As of September 2026 its published permit list doesn't name synthetic turf specifically, so a straightforward lawn conversion is worth a call before scheduling a crew. Our Polk County permit page covers the state rule and the county's own building division for context, but it's Dundee's own office, not the county's, that actually reviews an application inside town limits. Running a Dundee-area address through a parcel lookup on the county property appraiser's site settles whether it's inside town limits or unincorporated county before either call, and a Dundee HOA, where one exists still answers to the separate visibility statute covered on our HOA page, not the town's own permit process.

Questions people ask

What should the best artificial grass installer near me in Dundee already know about ridge lots?

Whether they've priced a Dundee job before: specifically, whether they know the town issues its own permits instead of Polk County, and whether they'll stake a 10-ft setback on a lake lot before ordering material. An installer who mentions the ridge sand's drainage without being asked has actually looked at the address.

Does the Town of Dundee or Polk County issue the permit for a backyard turf project?

Dundee's own Development Services Department does, at 124 Dundee Road, since the town runs its own building office rather than sending applications to the county. Our Polk County permit page still covers the state rule that applies inside Dundee, even though the county isn't who opens the file.

How many lakes does Dundee have, and does that change a turf project?

Eight lakes sit inside town limits, four of them open to the public. Lake Marie, Lake Menzie and Lake Annie come up most often on a residential job, and building within 10 feet of any of the three needs a seawall or bulkhead already standing in for the state's buffer.

What's the current watering schedule for Dundee's own water utility?

Dundee's addresses are down to one irrigation night a week under the Southwest Florida district's extreme-shortage order, even numbers on Tuesday and odd on Thursday, before 4 a.m. or after 8 p.m., a restriction the district extended through October 1, 2026. A capped synthetic lawn skips that schedule entirely.

Does new construction near Woodland Ranch Estates need a different turf base than an older Dundee lot?

The material is the same washed crushed rock either way, but a new-construction lot usually needs the builder's compacted grading broken up first, while an older in-town lot's undisturbed Candler sand mostly just needs shaping and compaction in proper lifts.
